publisher_body: Expert Group on Payment Fraud-related Topics (EGPF), created by the EBA in February 2020

license.name: CC BY 4.0
usage_conditions: Acknowledge the review and updating process and the expectation that updated versions are implemented effective 1 January following an annual review cycle, save emergency updates.
Adhere to the objective of a common pan-European fraud vocabulary without limitation on payment instrument type.

source_document.note: This JSON is a community-maintained machine-readable transcription of the official EBA Fraud Taxonomy PDF. The PDF published by the EBA is the sole authoritative source; this file is not itself an EBA publication.

objectives: Applies to both payment fraud and card fraud.
Creates a common vocabulary regarding fraud in the area of payments, building on definitions from authoritative and publicly available sources wherever possible.
Reduces the risk of overlap in the identification of fraud types, increasing the accuracy of statistics used to identify fraud trends.
Separates the contact method ('how') from the actual trick applied ('what'), supporting PSPs in developing effective fraud prevention campaigns.
Aligned with the EBA Guidelines on Fraud Reporting under PSD2.

fraud_definition.summary: Fraud comprises two branches, split by who initiated the payment transaction.

branches.name: Unauthorised payment transactions
branches.definition: Unauthorised payment transactions made, including as a result of the loss, theft or misappropriation of sensitive payment data or a payment instrument, whether detectable or not to the payer prior to a payment and whether or not caused by gross negligence of the payer or executed in the absence of consent by the payer.

branches.name: Manipulation of the payer
branches.definition: Payment transactions made as a result of the payer being manipulated by the fraudster to issue a payment order, or to give the instruction to do so to the payment service provider, in good faith, to a payment account it believes belongs to a legitimate payee.

fraud_definition.source: Guideline 1.1, EBA/GL/2018/05 (consolidated version), Guidelines on reporting requirements for fraud data under Article 96(6) PSD2

method.label: Method (how)
method.definition: Describes the attack vector and specifies the first point of contact between the fraudster and the victim or the point of compromise.

values.name: Brute force
values.definition: An exhaustive process to try and determine a cryptographic key, password or other secret credential by systematically trying all candidates or combinations until the correct one is discovered.

values.name: Data breach / theft
values.definition: A data breach is a security incident in which information is accessed without authorization. Data theft is the act of stealing information stored on corporate databases, devices, and servers.
values.source: Norton 'What is a data breach?' (data breach); Okta 'What is Data Theft?' (data theft)
values.example: Theft of customer data/credentials from a merchant database

values.name: Email contact
values.definition: The first point of contact was an e-mail message from the fraudster to the victim.

values.name: Fake advertising
values.definition: The fraudster has created advertisement, which lures victims in with false promises.
values.example: Direct advertisement in the form of banners and pop-ups; fraudulent web pages created to incentivise the victim to contact the fraudster

values.name: Fake merchant
values.definition: Fake merchant websites, for example offering non-existing goods or services to harvest personal details or banking/card details (honey trap), or to make the victim initiate a payment transaction.

values.name: In person contact
values.definition: The first point of contact was a person-to-person contact between the fraudster and the victim initiated by the fraudster.

values.name: Malware
values.definition: 'Malware' is short for malicious software and is used as a single term to refer to virus, spy ware, worm etc. Malware is designed to cause damage to a stand-alone computer or a networked PC. Wherever a malware term is used it means a program which is designed to damage your computer and it could refer to either a virus, worm or Trojan Horse.
values.source: Digicert 'What is Malware Viruses, Spyware, and Cookies?'
values.example: Modification of a payment order by the fraudster

values.name: Online contact
values.definition: Contact while connected to, served by, or available through a system and especially a computer or telecommunications system (such as the Internet). Usually initiated by the first-party fraudster with an online helpdesk or service centre at a financial institution.
values.example: Online credit card application, fraudulent disputes

values.name: Phone contact
values.definition: The first point of contact was a phone call by the fraudster to the victim.

values.name: Physical copy
values.definition: Creation of a physical duplicate or taking of a picture of a card or key card.

values.name: Physical theft
values.definition: Physical stealing of access credentials or device or whatever is needed to create fraud.

values.name: Social media contact
values.definition: The first point of contact was a message from the fraudster to the victim via a social media channel.

values.name: Text message contact
values.definition: The first point of contact was a text message from the fraudster to the victim sent through a (pure) text messaging functionality/app.
values.note: Includes any form of pure text that is designed for messaging.

values.name: New method
values.definition: Used to register a new method of contact / attack vector not yet included in the list of methods.

initiator.label: Initiator (who)
initiator.definition: Describes who initiates the payment transaction affected by the fraud, i.e. the customer or the fraudster. Aligned with EBA Guidelines on Fraud Reporting under PSD2.

values.name: Customer
values.definition: Manipulation of the payer by the fraudster to issue a payment order (payer initiates, in good faith, having been manipulated).
values.example: Manipulation of the customer into initiating and signing off a payment order

values.name: Fraudster
values.definition: Issuance of a payment order by the fraudster, covers both modification of a legitimate payment order in transit (e.g. man-in-the-middle) and issuance of a fake payment order after obtaining the payer/payee's sensitive payment data through fraudulent means.
values.example: Initiation and sign-off of a payment order by the fraudster

values.name: First party
values.definition: A person knowingly misrepresents their identity or gives false information for financial or material gain. Optional element, relevant in particular to card fraud.
values.source: Experian 'The different types of fraud and how they're changing'

modus.label: Modus (what)
modus.definition: Describes the unauthorised and often manipulative action taken by the fraudster and resulting in the loss of money via a payment transaction. Clustered within high-level classifications reflecting the fraudster's strategic approach.

high_level_classifications.name: Your money / personal information is at risk
high_level_classifications.definition: Fraudster tricks victim into believing that an intervention is needed to keep their money / personal information safe.

modi.name: Safe account fraud
modi.definition: You'll be contacted, usually on the phone by someone claiming to be from your bank's fraud department, the police or a regulatory body (...). They'll say your account has been compromised in some way and encourage you to transfer all your money from your bank to a 'safe account' they control. Alternatively/additionally, this modus could result in the victim handing over account credentials or a physical/virtual card or card details and/or completing authentication steps required to access the account and/or sign off payment transactions.

modi.name: Stop unauthorised transaction fraud
modi.definition: The fraudster impersonates a representative of a payment service provider, law enforcement, or a public authority. The fraudster tells the PSP's customer that an unauthorised transaction can be blocked by giving out authentication codes and/or signing off transactions and/or sending money.

modi.name: Stop unauthorised access fraud
modi.definition: The fraudster impersonates a representative of a payment service provider, law enforcement, or a public authority. The fraudster tells the PSP's customer that someone has gained unauthorised access to the customer's accounts and therefore the customer would be exposed to multiple risks. The fraudster convinces the customer that this unauthorised access can be addressed by the customer authenticating themselves or providing authentication codes.

high_level_classifications.name: You can earn/save a lot of money
high_level_classifications.definition: Victim makes payment up front in expectation of a return at a later stage.

modi.name: Advance fee fraud
modi.definition: Advance fee fraud is when fraudsters target victims to make advance or upfront payments for goods, services and/or financial gains that do not materialise. Alternatively/additionally, this modus could result in the victim handing over account credentials or a physical/virtual card or card details and/or completing authentication steps required to access the account and/or sign off payment transactions.
modi.source: National Fraud & Cyber Crime Reporting Centre 'Advance Fee Fraud'
possible_labels_tags: Fake prize, sweepstakes, and lottery fraud

modi.name: Claim a benefit fraud
modi.definition: The aim of this type of fraud is to deceive victims into handing over account credentials or card details and/or completing authentication steps required to access the account and/or sign off payment transactions to claim a reward or benefits, such as lottery wins, discounts or reimbursements.
possible_labels_tags: Fake prize, sweepstakes, and lottery fraud

modi.name: Investment fraud
modi.definition: Investment scams promise big returns, but the goal is stealing money. Scammers use convincing marketing and new technology to make their investment sound too good to miss, promising big payouts with little or no risk and using pressure tactics to get victims to act fast.
possible_labels_tags: Fraudulent use of Contract for Difference (CFD)

high_level_classifications.name: I am a seller/buyer
high_level_classifications.definition: Victim responds to fake/alleged offer for services/goods that later turns out to be fraudulent.

modi.name: Online shopping fraud
modi.definition: Shopping and auction fraud involves fraudulent shopping scams that rely on the anonymity of the internet.
examples: Buyers receiving goods less valuable than or significantly different from the original description
Failure to disclose relevant information about a product or the terms of sale

high_level_classifications.name: Please help
high_level_classifications.definition: Fraudster creates an emotional bond with the victim, typically friendship/sympathy/romantic, then exploits the bond by getting the victim to help the fraudster financially. Alternatively, the fraudster invents an emergency scenario requiring the victim to provide financial assistance to a family member or friend.

modi.name: Emotional manipulation
modi.definition: Emotional manipulation is considered to be the ability to influence another individual's feelings and behaviors for one's own self-interest or benefit. The victim is tricked into providing, for example, money or gifts. Alternatively/additionally, this modus could result in the victim handing over account credentials or a physical/virtual card or card details and/or completing authentication steps required to access the account and/or sign off payment transactions.
modi.source: Hyde, J. & Grieve, R. (2014). Able and willing: Refining the measurement of emotional manipulation
modi.possible_labels_tags_note: The v6.0 PDF lists this label as 'Shock call'; the labels/tags section of the same document spells it 'Shock calls'. Normalised to the labels/tags spelling.

high_level_classifications.name: Send me money or I'll ...
high_level_classifications.definition: Fraudster extorts e.g. money from victim, based on exposure threat, blackmail or other, like ransomware.

modi.name: Extortion
modi.definition: Scammers threaten you so you will pay them money. They may threaten you with arrest, deportation, or even physical harm, if you don't agree to pay them immediately. Alternatively/additionally, could result in the victim handing over account credentials, a card or card details, and/or completing authentication steps.
modi.source: National Anti-Scam Centre 'Threats and extortion scams'

high_level_classifications.name: We've changed account number
high_level_classifications.definition: Victim misled into replacing genuine static account details of a creditor with details of an account under control of a fraudster.

modi.name: Impersonation of creditor
modi.definition: A fraudster impersonates a service provider, supplier or other creditor and tricks the victim into making a bill payment to an account that is not the account of the actual creditor but the account of the fraudster.

high_level_classifications.name: Comply with payment obligation
high_level_classifications.definition: Fraudster makes victim believe that money is owed or due, usually in relation to completely fictitious transactions or payments. Alternatively, the fraudster pretends to be a person with authority to instruct the victim to execute a payment transaction.

modi.name: Impersonation of person with authority to instruct payments
modi.definition: The fraudster impersonates a person with authority to instruct the victim to make payment(s) to a third party designated by the fraudster.

modi.name: Overpayment fraud
modi.definition: Overpayment fraud involves a buyer paying a seller more than an item is worth and/or more than a seller is asking for. The buyer sends a check or a money order, asking the seller to send back the overpayment. The seller returns the excess money, but it turns out that the initial money order or check was fraudulent.
modi.possible_labels_tags_note: The PDF annotates this label for this modus: scammer paid with a lost or stolen card.

modi.name: Phoney debt/bill collection
modi.definition: Aggressive fake debt collectors, who try to bully their targets into paying money they don't owe.

high_level_classifications.name: Can you please sign in / sign this off?
high_level_classifications.definition: Fraudster tricks customer into giving out authentication codes for seemingly legitimate reasons not related to bank activity.

modi.name: Fake institution
modi.definition: The fraudster impersonates or claims to act on behalf of an institution like a health care provider, a government agency or a payment service provider. The fraudster asks the victim to provide authentication data and/or go through authentication steps in order to e.g. identify themselves, sign in to retrieve information, sign (off) something, or confirm something. The victims believe that they are resolving a legitimate issue by engaging with the fraudster.

high_level_classifications.name: Account / card / card details / digital wallet takeover by unauthorised party
high_level_classifications.definition: A situation where the fraudster obtains control, without the victim being involved or aware, over the victim's account, card, card details or digital wallet allowing the fraudster to issue payment transactions through the victim's account, card or digital wallet.

modi.name: Pure account takeover
modi.definition: An account takeover can happen when a fraudster or computer criminal poses as a genuine customer, gains control of an account and makes unauthorised transactions. Online banking accounts are usually taken over as a result of phishing, spyware or malware scams. Pure account takeover is a form of account takeover where the fraudster gains access to the account without tricking the victim into a handover of credentials.
examples: Account takeover via compromised digital wallet
possible_labels_tags: Physical proximity credential theft / known perpetrator
Physical proximity credential theft / unknown perpetrator
modi.possible_labels_tags_note: The PDF lists the generic 'Physical proximity credential theft'; the labels/tags section defines two variants, both listed here.

modi.name: Creditor account data manipulation
modi.definition: Creditor account data manipulation occurs if, following an account takeover, the fraudster changes creditor account data stored in this account so that future transactions reach the wrong beneficiaries.

modi.name: Control of card or card details by unauthorised party
modi.definition: Fraudster gains control of the victim's physical or virtual card or card details without tricking the victim into a handover of the card or the card details.

high_level_classifications.name: First party fraud
high_level_classifications.definition: A situation where a person knowingly misrepresents their identity or gives false information for financial or material gain.
high_level_classifications.note: Included for exploration and internal reporting purposes only, not for fraud intelligence sharing.
high_level_classifications.source: Experian 'The different types of fraud and how they're changing'

modi.name: Fraudulent card application
modi.definition: When a fraudster uses another person's name and information to apply for and obtain a credit card.
modi.source: Digital News Asia 'The 8 Different Types of Card Fraud'

modi.name: Fraudulent card claim
modi.definition: The fraudster files a false credit card dispute claim, e.g. false chargebacks. Chargeback abuse occurs if a buyer files a chargeback claim that's not tied to one of the valid reasons, also known as first-party or 'friendly' fraud.
modi.example: Impersonating the victim or pretending to be a victim, the fraudster presents a fraudulent claim to the bank.

modi.name: Fraudulent use of cash back scheme
modi.definition: Fraudulent use of cash back schemes involves fake transactions between merchants and employees to make undue gains from cashback offers.
modi.source: Global Banking & Finance Review 'What is cash back?'

modi.name: Other first party fraud
modi.definition: Incidents of first party fraud not related to card fraud, e.g. mortgage fraud or lending fraud.

catch_all.name: New fraud type (describe)
catch_all.definition: Used to register new modus not yet included in the list of modi.

labels_tags.label: Labels/tags (what else) (PSP individual)
labels_tags.definition: Optional, non-exhaustive suggestions to enrich a case with additional categorisation information on a voluntary basis. Individual PSPs remain free to choose labels/tags as they deem fit, for example to align with internal reporting requirements.

values.name: Account takeover
values.definition: Account takeover fraud is a form of identity theft in which the fraudster gets access to a victim's bank or credit card accounts, through a data breach, malware or phishing, and uses them to make unauthorized transactions.

values.name: Advanced persistent threat (APT)
values.definition: A covert cyber attack on a computer network where the attacker gains and maintains unauthorized access to the targeted network and remains undetected for a significant period.

values.name: Beneficiary account change
values.definition: A request to change the details of a beneficiary's account to which payments are made. A fraudster exploits weaknesses in a genuine change request process, changing genuine beneficiary account details to those of an account he holds.
values.source: Citibank 'Beneficiary Change Request: Risks and Best Practices'

values.name: BIN attack
values.definition: Credit cards are produced in BIN ranges. Where an issuer does not use random generation of the card number, it is possible for an attacker to obtain one good card number and generate valid card numbers.
values.source: European Association for Secure Transactions (EAST) 'Fraud Definitions'

values.name: Card details stolen
values.definition: Involves the unauthorised use of credit or debit card data (card number, billing address, security code, expiry date) to purchase products and services in a non-face-to-face setting, such as via e-commerce websites or over the telephone.

values.name: Card lost
values.definition: Fraud carried out on cards that have been lost.

values.name: Card never received
values.definition: When a new or replacement card is stolen from the mail, never reaching its rightful owner.
values.source: Digital News Asia 'The 8 Different Types of Card Fraud'

values.name: Card not present
values.definition: A card not present transaction (CNP, MO/TO, Mail Order / Telephone Order, MOTOEC) is a payment card transaction made where the cardholder does not or cannot physically present the card for a merchant's visual examination at the time an order is given and payment effected.
values.source: European Association for Secure Transactions (EAST) 'Fraud Definitions'

values.name: Card peeking
values.definition: Card details stolen by someone who has physical access to the card. The card remains in the possession of the cardholder.
values.example: An employee has their business card stored in their office drawer. A colleague is able to get necessary card information without stealing the physical card.

values.name: Card present
values.definition: A card present transaction occurs when a cardholder physically presents a card to request and authorise a financial transaction.
values.source: European Association for Secure Transactions (EAST) 'Fraud Definitions'

values.name: Card skimming
values.definition: Skimming occurs when devices are illegally installed on or inside ATMs, point-of-sale (POS) terminals, or fuel pumps to capture card data and record cardholders' PIN entries. Criminals use the data to create fake debit or credit cards and then steal from victims' accounts.

values.name: Card stolen
values.definition: Various ways criminals try to steal cards: intercepting new cards or PINs in the post, handbag or wallet snatches, shoulder surfing, distraction theft.

values.name: CEO fraud
values.definition: CEO fraud will typically start with an email being sent from a fraudster to a member of staff in a company's finance department. The member of staff will be told by the fraudster who is purporting to be a company director or CEO that they need to quickly transfer money to a certain bank account for a specific reason. The member of staff will do as their boss has instructed, only to find that they have sent money to a fraudster's bank account. The fraudster will normally redistribute this money into other mule accounts and then close down the bank account to make it untraceable.
values.source: National Fraud & Cyber Crime Reporting Centre 'Action Fraud warning after serious rise in CEO fraud'

values.name: Collusive merchant / data misuse
values.definition: Occurs when merchant owners and/or their employees conspire to commit fraud using their customers' (cardholder) accounts and/or personal information, merchant owners and/or their employees pass on the information about cardholders to fraudsters.
values.source: International Journal of Advanced Research in Computer Science and Software Engineering, Vol. 3, Issue 6, 2013
values.example: Could also occur by abusing existing direct debit mandates or issuing new direct debit mandates.

values.name: Contactless relay fraud
values.definition: Where a fraudster uses a mobile NFC POS terminal or smartphone to capture a payment by standing very close to the cardholder and reading their contactless card through their clothing or handbag.

values.name: Credit master
values.definition: Algorithms are deployed which automatically generate credit card account numbers from an existing correct number as well as pairs of expiration dates. The criminal software then automatically tests these combinations, working sequentially through number combinations to see which match genuine cards by attempting a transaction.

values.name: Discount / refund fraud
values.definition: The fraudster impersonates customer support and convinces the victim that they are entitled to a discount, but they just have to authenticate themselves first, thus giving the fraudster access to their account and/or signing off unauthorised transactions.

values.name: Email compromise
values.definition: Use of a hacked or spoofed e-mail address to gain access to other parties for fraudulent purposes. Business E-mail Compromise (BEC) is a sophisticated scam targeting businesses working with foreign suppliers and/or businesses that regularly perform wire transfer payments.

values.name: Exploiting the system
values.definition: The cardholder is trying to benefit and avoid paying for goods/services by filing a dispute and using the chargeback system.

values.name: Fake bank / financial institution
values.definition: A bank impersonation scam is when a scammer makes direct contact with the victim while impersonating a trusted bank, to gain access to their personal information and/or money.
values.source: ANZ 'What is a bank impersonation scam, and how can you protect yourself?'

values.name: Fake betting
values.definition: These scams are a form of gambling made to look like real investments. (...) Betting syndicates: The scammer asks you to become a member of a betting syndicate for a joining fee. (...) You are required to make ongoing deposits to maintain the balance of the account. The scammer tells you that they will use funds in the account to place bets on behalf of the syndicate. You, and other 'syndicate members' are promised a percentage of the profits.
values.source: National Anti-Scam Centre 'Investment scams / Gambling and sports betting scams'

values.name: Fake customer support
values.definition: Fraudster impersonates customer support. The scammer will phone you and pretend to be a staff member from a large telecommunications or computer company (...). Alternatively they may claim to be from a technical support service provider. They will tell you that your computer has been sending error messages or that it has a virus. (...) The caller will request remote access to your computer to 'find out what the problem is'. The scammer may try to talk you into buying unnecessary software or a service to 'fix' the computer, or they may ask you for your personal details and your bank or credit card details.

values.name: Fake loan
values.definition: In an advance-fee loan scam, scammers promise a loan, credit card, or access to credit, but first require an upfront fee. There is no loan, and the scammer disappears with the money.
values.source: US Federal Trade Commission 'What To Know About Advance-Fee Loans'

values.name: Fake police
values.definition: To identify yourself as an officer of the law to purposefully deceive other individuals and gain advantage through such deceit. Impersonation may include dressing as an officer of the law or simply falsely identifying oneself as an officer to someone else.

values.name: Fake prize, sweepstakes, and lottery fraud
values.definition: Fraudsters contact you to tell you you've won a large sum of money in an international lottery, sweepstake or other prize draw. The lottery doesn't exist or a genuine lottery's name is misused. If you respond, you're asked to supply personal information and copies of official documents, then asked to pay various fees so they can 'release' your non-existent winnings.

values.name: Fake website
values.definition: Fake sites made to look like real ones to steal your personal or banking details when you submit them to the site.

values.name: False billing fraud
values.definition: False billing scams target you or your business with fake invoices for a variety of normal business supplies and activities including directory listings, advertising, domain name renewals or office supplies, hoping accounts staff will pay quickly without examining the fraudulent details.
values.source: Northern Territory Consumer Affairs 'False billing scams'

values.name: Falsified ID
values.definition: A false or fake ID is any form of identification that is forged, altered, or otherwise purports to establish the false identity of a person.
values.source: Criminal Defense Lawyer 'Fake ID: Laws and Penalties'

values.name: Falsifying personal and financial information
values.definition: The act of deliberately lying about or misrepresenting something.

values.name: Family emergency
values.definition: Someone calls or contacts you saying they are a family member or close friend. They say they need money to get out of trouble.
values.source: US Federal Trade Commission 'Scammers Use Fake Emergencies To Steal Your Money'

values.name: Fraudulent MOTO card transaction
values.definition: Fraud in so-called 'card-not-present' transactions online or via email order and telephone transactions.
values.source: Digital News Asia 'The 8 Different Types of Card Fraud'

values.name: Fraudulent use of Contract for Difference (CFD)
values.definition: Contracts for difference (CFD) are a popular way of trading on the price of stocks and indices, commodities, forex and cryptocurrencies without owning the underlying assets. (...) A CFD is a contract between a broker and a trader who agree to exchange the difference in value of an underlying security between the beginning and the end of the contract, often less than one day.
values.source: Capital.com 'What is CFD trading and how does it work?'

values.name: Fraudulent use of crypto currency
values.definition: Cryptocurrency is a type of digital currency that generally exists only electronically. With investment scams, crypto is central in two ways: it can be both the investment and the payment.
values.source: US Federal Trade Commission 'What To Know About Cryptocurrency and Scams'
values.example: Fraudster pretends to represent a legitimate company offering an opportunity to invest into crypto currency; customer directed to a fake website and tricked into setting up an account; once the customer wishes to liquidate, the funds are gone.

values.name: Gift card
values.definition: Scammers like to get gift cards as payment as it's easy for them to quickly sell them on secondary markets and pocket the cash.
values.source: National Anti-Scam Centre 'Payment demanded by gift card? It's a scam'

values.name: Goods not received
values.definition: Payer submitted payment, however does not receive the purchased goods, because the offer was issued on a fake website store or by a fake seller.
values.source: National Anti-Scam Centre "'Tis the season for online shopping scams"

values.name: Impersonation
values.definition: The act of attempting to deceive someone by pretending that you are another person.

values.name: Keylogger
values.definition: A keylogger (or keystroke logger) is a type of spyware that monitors and records what you type on your computer or mobile phone.

values.name: Lookalike domain
values.definition: Lookalike or 'cousin' domain names are addresses that use character replacement to make them look as close as possible to the domain of a brand, service or government authority.
values.example: Fraudsters create domains very similar to an existing business/financial institution's name to collect sign-in credentials for online payment or shopping accounts.

values.name: Malware – MageCart
values.definition: Magecart is a consortium of malicious hacker groups who target online shopping cart systems, usually the Magento system, to steal customer payment card information, a supply chain attack compromising a third-party piece of software from a VAR or systems integrator.
values.source: CSO 'What is Magecart? How this hacker group steals payment card data'

values.name: Manipulated invoice
values.definition: A contractor or supplier can commit fraud by knowingly submitting false, inflated or duplicate invoices with the intent to defraud, either acting alone or in collusion with contracting personnel.
values.source: Guide to Combating Corruption & Fraud in Development Projects

values.name: Multiple imprint
values.definition: When a single transaction is recorded multiple times on old-fashioned credit card imprint machines known as 'knuckle busters'.
values.source: Digital News Asia 'The 8 Different Types of Card Fraud'

values.name: Nigeria
values.definition: In a Nigerian scam, a scammer from abroad offers via mail the target a portion of a sizable quantity of money in exchange for helping them move the money out of his native country to his current place.

values.name: Nightclub
values.definition: Clip joint fraud or nightclub fraud, where customers are threatened by a nightclub they have visited into making payments.

values.name: No physical meeting
values.definition: E.g. reunion exclusively using a digital communication channel.

values.name: Non-crypto investment fraud
values.definition: You search online for bonds, shares or pension plans, then someone contacts you with an investment deal. They might say you need to pay a fee to secure it. Eventually they'll disappear with the fee and any money invested.

values.name: Phishing
values.definition: Technique of fraudulently obtaining private information. Typically, the phisher sends an e-mail that appears to come from a legitimate business, requesting 'verification' of information and warning of some dire consequence if not provided. The e-mail usually contains a link to a fraudulent web page that seems legitimate.
values.source: European Association for Secure Transactions (EAST) 'Fraud Definitions'

values.name: Physical meeting
values.definition: Face-to-face reunion.

values.name: Physical proximity credential theft / known perpetrator
values.definition: Credential theft where the perpetrator is known to the victim.
values.example: A family member, family friend or caretaker who has been in the vicinity of the victim and e.g. takes a photo of the victim's payment card.

values.name: Physical proximity credential theft / unknown perpetrator
values.definition: Credential theft where the perpetrator is not known to the victim.
values.example: A person not known to the victim steals the victim's payment card, e.g. from a locker in the gym.

values.name: Ransomware
values.definition: Ransomware is malware that employs encryption to hold a victim's information at ransom. A user or organization's critical data is encrypted so that they cannot access files, databases, or applications. A ransom is then demanded to provide access.

values.name: Remote access trojan
values.definition: A malicious program that remotely accesses infected resources. RATs are among the most dangerous because they open up all kinds of opportunities for remote control of the compromised system, including installation/removal, file manipulation, reading data from the keyboard, webcam hijacking, and clipboard monitoring.

values.name: Romance fraud
values.definition: Scammers use dating or friendship to win your trust and get your money. Scammers use social media, dating or gaming apps and websites to find people looking for love and friendship. They create fake profiles, sometimes of famous people. They might also call or message a lot to make you feel special. This is sometimes called 'love bombing'. Once you trust them, they might tell you about an urgent problem they need your money for. They might ask you to set up accounts or transfer money they give you. Or they might convince you to use cryptocurrency and invest in a fake scheme they say is real. Either way, the scammer steals your money and disappears, and you don't get it back.

became_modus_in.note: Moved from labels/tags to the modus section in 7.0. Its definition and cited URL also changed at that point (romance-scams became relationship-scams).

values.name: Sextortion
values.definition: Scammers use social media platforms and email as forums for sextortion scams, where they threaten to share intimate images or footage of you online, unless you give in to their demands.
values.source: National Anti-Scam Centre 'Gen Z the fastest growing victims of scams'

values.name: Shock calls
values.definition: The fraudster contacts the victim impersonating, for example, a representative of law enforcement or a health service, claiming a family member had been involved in an accident and that the victim must post bail for their release.
values.source: Europol 'Police track down criminal network behind shock calls terrifying elderly across Europe'

values.name: Shoulder surfing
values.definition: Shoulder surfing is when identity thieves glance over your shoulder and steal your personal data, such as your login details for a bank or credit card account or bank PIN.

values.name: Smishing
values.definition: A form of criminal activity using social engineering techniques. SMS phishing uses cell phone text messages to deliver information and/or requests to induce people to divulge or take action that will compromise their personal or confidential information.
values.source: European Association for Secure Transactions (EAST) 'Fraud Definitions'

values.name: Social media compromise
values.definition: Use of hacked, spoofed or stolen social media accounts to gain access to other parties for fraudulent purposes.

values.name: Spoofed email
values.definition: Email spoofing is a deceptive technique used to make an email appear as if it's from a trusted source, like a friend or legitimate organization. Scammers commonly use spoofed email addresses in phishing attacks to trick recipients into sharing sensitive personal information or clicking dangerous links.
values.source: Norton 'What is email spoofing? A complete guide'

values.name: Subscription fraud
values.definition: Some online subscription companies employ confusing business tactics, such as opting customers into recurring charges without their knowledge.

values.name: Synthetic ID
values.definition: Synthetic identity theft is an advanced form of identity theft that involves using a mix of real and fake information to create a fictitious identity, which scammers can then use to open bank accounts, apply for loans, or commit other types of financial fraud. Especially challenging to detect because it blends valid data, like Social Security numbers or addresses, with fabricated details.

values.name: Third-party channel
values.definition: The fraudster used a third-party channel under PSD2 to initiate the payment.

values.name: Third-party vendor account takeover
values.definition: The fraudster is able to log into an online account held by the customer with a third party, i.e. a vendor, where payment information (e.g. card details) is stored. This enables the fraudster to consume digital goods/services or order merchandise and redirect its delivery to their own address.

values.name: Use of counterfeit cards
values.definition: A counterfeit card is a bogus replica of a legitimate credit or debit card, usually created from stolen card information. These fake cards are designed to mimic the appearance and functionality of actual payment cards.

values.name: Vishing
values.definition: The criminal practice of using social engineering over the telephone system to gain access to private personal and financial information from the public. Also employed by attackers for reconnaissance purposes to gather more detailed intelligence on a target organisation.
values.source: European Association for Secure Transactions (EAST) 'Fraud Definitions'

values.name: Wecycle
values.definition: A trend in debit card fraud, emails sent to consumers asking them to send in expired debit cards. The email contains a link to an online form where consumers enter personal information before receiving instructions on where to send the debit card for recycling, so fraudsters can easily get their hands on the victim's money.
values.source: NL Times 'Warning issued over new debit card fraud'

payment_instrument.label: Payment instrument (optional)
payment_instrument.definition: Optional element to identify whether the fraudulent payment was an account-to-account transaction or a card payment.

values.name: Account-to-account transaction
values.definition: Account-to-account payments move money directly from a payer's bank account to a payee's bank account without the need for intermediaries, such as credit or debit cards.

values.name: Card payment
values.definition: Card payments are a cashless payment method where customers pay for their purchases with their debit or credit card, either via a point of sale (POS) or online.

change_types.added: A new entry with no predecessor. Consumers add it.
change_types.retired: An entry removed with no successor. Its code is retained and never reused. Records classified under an earlier version stay valid.
change_types.split: One entry replaced by several. Successors carry derived_from; the predecessor carries superseded_by. A trend series on the predecessor continues as the sum of its successors.
change_types.merged: Several entries replaced by one. The survivor carries derived_from listing each predecessor.
change_types.renamed: Same concept, different name. The code does not change, so stored records need no migration.
change_types.moved: Same concept, different dimension (for example a label/tag becoming a modus). The code changes because code namespaces are per dimension; the entry carries moved_from.
change_types.redefined: The meaning of an entry changed. This is the only change type that can require re-classification of existing records.
change_types.recited: The definition text was replaced with an equivalent from a different source. The meaning did not change and no re-classification is required.

compatibility.principle: A record is classified under one version and carries that version. Consumers must expect to receive records classified under a version other than the one they run, because the taxonomy is republished annually with a six-month lead time and adopters do not all move on the same day. The rules below let a consumer interpret such a record instead of rejecting it.
compatibility.code_stability: Codes are the unit of compatibility. A code is assigned once and never renumbered or reused, including after retirement. A code therefore denotes the same concept in every version in which it appears, and any two versions can be related to each other through the lineage fields rather than through name matching.

backward.meaning: A consumer on a newer version reading a record classified under an older version.
backward.rule: Resolve the record's codes against the older version. Codes that still exist are read directly. A code that has since been retired is found in the dimension's retired array; its superseded_by list gives the successors. Do not rewrite the stored record: interpret it, and keep the original version stamp.
backward.worked_example: A record classified under an earlier version carrying the modus that became D024 is read by a 7.0 consumer as 'one of D008, D009, D010'. Which one is not recoverable from the record alone, because the split added information that the original classification did not contain.

forward.meaning: A consumer on an older version reading a record classified under a newer version.
forward.rule: An unrecognised code must not be discarded and must not be treated as invalid. Widen it: follow derived_from to the predecessor the consumer does know, and failing that fall back to the code's high-level classification group, which is coarser but stable. Record that the value was widened.
forward.worked_example: A consumer that predates 7.0 receives D009. It does not know that code. derived_from resolves to D024, which it does know, so the record is read at that coarser level without loss of validity.

compatibility.unknown_code_rule: Widen, never drop and never guess. Dropping an unknown code silently loses a case from every downstream count; guessing a sibling code invents data. Widening is lossy in precision but never wrong, and it is visible because the widening is recorded.

lossiness.exact: One code maps to one code. Safe in both directions. This is the case for every entry that did not change, and also for entries whose definition was only recited, since recitation does not change meaning.
lossiness.widening: Several codes map to one coarser code. Safe: counts roll up without loss. This is the direction that keeps a trend series continuous across a split.
lossiness.narrowing: One code maps to several finer codes. Not automatically resolvable. The finer distinction was not present in the original record and cannot be recovered from it. Either keep the record at the coarser level or re-classify the case from its source material.

compatibility.trend_series: To carry a series across a split, sum the successors and attribute the total to the predecessor code. changes and the retired arrays carry what is needed to do this mechanically. The alternative, keying a series on names, breaks silently at every rename.
compatibility.schema_versioning: schema.json pins exactly one taxonomy version, deliberately, so that validation is unambiguous about what a record claims to be. A consumer that must accept several versions should keep one generated schema per version and select by the record's taxonomy_version field, rather than loosening a single schema to accept everything. Tag each release of this repository so previous schemas stay retrievable.
compatibility.current_state: This repository currently carries version 7.0 only. The codes in it are assigned by this repository; the EBA's published PDF does not define codes. There is therefore no earlier code table to map from yet. The mechanism above is defined now, and demonstrated against the 6.0 to 7.0 change recorded in 'changes', so that it is already in place when a second version is published. Transcribing 6.0 would make the mapping concrete in both directions.

steps.detail: EBA invites change requests from EGPF members, fraud experts of EBA member organisations, and organisations with usage rights, via a standard form.
Specific deadline agreed by the EGPF each year.
Change requests must specify the proposed naming and definition of the new label.
The EGPF reviews change requests received; non-member submitting organisations are invited to join the relevant EGPF meeting.
The EBA Board adopts an updated version of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy.
The EBA communicates the updated version to EGPF members, fraud experts and organisations with usage rights.
Six-month lead time; effective 1 January of the next calendar year.

review_and_updating_process.emergency_change_process: May be triggered when exceptional circumstances require immediate amendments (e.g. regulatory requirements, or fraud developments with a high degree of proliferation and potential large-scale impact); steps to adoption may be expedited.

lifecycle_note: This is the 6.0 snapshot, transcribed in the same shape as 7.0. Codes are shared across versions: an entry keeps the same code in every version it appears in. Entries present here but not in 7.0 appear in 7.0 under dimensions.<name>.retired. introduced_in is '<=6.0' throughout because the versions before 6.0 have not been transcribed; it does not mean the entry was introduced in 6.0.
codes_design_note: Codes are intentionally opaque (for example 'D014', not 'romance_fraud'). Two reasons. First, a human-readable value in the machine field can bias a reviewer before they have read the definition. Second, names can change between annual versions while codes must not. Use code for storage and interchange, and name for display only. Once published, a code is never renumbered or reused: a retired entry keeps its code and is listed under dimensions.modus.retired with superseded_by, and each superseding entry carries derived_from, so trend series can be bridged across a split or rename instead of silently dropping to zero.
definitions_note: Definitions are transcribed from the EBA Fraud Taxonomy v7.0 PDF. Where the EBA quotes a third-party source, this file reproduces the quotation with its attribution, but some quotations are shortened; those entries carry abridged: true. Ellipses that appear in the PDF's own quotations are the EBA's. For the exact quoted text, consult the PDF, which is the sole authoritative version.
